segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the assembly of God that is in Corinth, together with all the holy ones who are in the whole of Achaia:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we can comfort those in any affliction with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so through Christ our comfort overflows as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which takes effect as you endure the same sufferings that we also suffer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And our hope for you is firm, because we know that as you share in the sufferings, so you share also in the comfort.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, of the affliction that came upon us in Asia: we were weighed down so excessively, beyond our strength, that we despaired even of living.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Indeed, we ourselves had the sentence of death within us, so that we would trust not in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He rescued us from so great a death, and he will rescue us; on him we have set our hope that he will rescue us yet again,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as you too join in helping by praying for us, so that many people may give thanks on our behalf for the gift granted to us through many.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience: that we have conducted ourselves in the world, and all the more toward you, with the holiness and sincerity that come from God, not by fleshly wisdom but by the grace of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we write you nothing other than what you read and indeed understand, and I hope that you will understand fully,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as you have also understood us in part—that we are your boast, just as you are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In this confidence I intended to come to you first, so that you might have a second favor,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to go on through you to Macedonia, and from Macedonia to come back to you and be sent on my way by you to Judea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when I intended this, was I being fickle? Or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me it is both “Yes, yes” and “No, no”?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as God is faithful, our word to you is not “Yes and No.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you by us—by me and Silvanus and Timothy—was not “Yes and No”; rather, in him it has been “Yes.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For however many God’s promises are, in him is the “Yes.” That is why it is also through him that the “Amen” is spoken by us to God for his glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now it is God who makes us firm with you in Christ and who anointed us,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who also sealed us and gave us the Spirit in our hearts as a down payment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I call on God as my witness, on my life, that it was to spare you that I did not come again to Corinth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not that we lord it over your faith; rather, we are coworkers for your joy, for it is by faith that you stand.

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one word wherever the Greek has one.

The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” is the traditional rendering and many translations keep it, but it now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other versions use “God’s people” or “his holy people.”

The noun and its verb occur ten times in verses 3–7, and the repetition is kept in English. The Greek word covers both consoling and strengthening, so “encouragement” is also possible. It echoes the Septuagint’s language for God comforting his people, as in Isaiah 40:1.

The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole community. “Brothers” alone now sounds as though only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep “brothers” with a footnote.

Some manuscripts read a present tense here (“and does rescue”), which lies behind the King James Version’s past, present and future sequence. The earliest witnesses have the future, and a few omit the phrase altogether. The future is the reading most editors prefer, even though it repeats the following clause.

notes.traditional: by the means of many persons
notes.note: The Greek sentence is compressed and can be construed in more than one way. Here “through many” is taken with the gift, meaning that God’s rescue came in answer to the prayers of many. It could instead go with the thanksgiving (“thanks may be given by many”), and the phrase rendered “many people” is literally “many faces,” perhaps picturing faces turned up in prayer.

Manuscripts are divided between “holiness” and a similar-looking Greek word meaning “simplicity” or “frankness.” The latter suits the context of Paul defending his straightforwardness and is preferred by some editors and translations. The Greek text translated here reads “holiness,” which has strong early support.

In Paul’s usage “flesh” often stands for human nature left to its own resources, apart from God, and not specifically for the body or its appetites. “Fleshly wisdom” is therefore merely human shrewdness, and “according to the flesh” in verse 17 means planning by self-interested human calculation. Some translations paraphrase as “worldly” or “earthly” wisdom.

The Greek phrase can mean “to the end” (in time, until the day of the Lord mentioned in verse 14) or “completely.” The contrast with “in part” in the next verse favors “fully,” but both readings are well supported. The sentence also plays on two similar Greek verbs, “read” and “understand,” which English cannot reproduce.

The word is the one usually rendered “grace”; here it refers to the benefit the Corinthians would receive from a second visit, though some take it as a second occasion of divine grace. A number of manuscripts read a similar word meaning “joy.” Paul’s plan was to visit Corinth both on the way to Macedonia and on the way back.

There is a wordplay in the Greek: “Christ” (Christos) means “anointed one,” and the verb “anointed” (chrisas) follows immediately. The terms in verses 21–22 for making firm, sealing and giving a down payment were also used in commerce for guaranteeing a transaction, so Paul describes God as standing surety for his people.

The word is a commercial term for a first installment that secures a transaction and obliges the payer to complete it. “Earnest” is no longer understood in this sense, and “guarantee” loses the idea that part of the payment has already been made. The Spirit is itself the down payment: the Greek is literally “the down payment of the Spirit.”

Paul swears an oath, inviting God to act against him if he is lying. The Greek word traditionally rendered “soul” here means his life or his very self, which is what he stakes on the truth of his statement. Several modern versions paraphrase as “against me.”

candidates.reason: With its verb παρακαλέω it ranges over comfort, encouragement, exhortation and appeal across the New Testament, and translators divide between “comfort,” “consolation” and “encouragement” even within one passage.
Paul’s κατὰ σάρκα and σαρκικός recur across the letters and versions vary between “flesh,” “worldly,” “human” and “sinful nature,” hiding that one word is in play.
Occurs at 2 Cor 1:22, 5:5 and Eph 1:14 with versions split among “earnest,” “guarantee,” “deposit,” “pledge” and “down payment”; one rendering should serve all three.
The plural address to mixed communities occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and the choice between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters” needs to be uniform.
The καυχάομαι word group is thematic in 2 Corinthians and Romans, and versions vary between “boast,” “pride,” “glory” and “rejoice,” obscuring the thread.
